title: Al-Razi the physician
hookLine: the physician who told smallpox from measles and ran Baghdad's hospital

cards: Baghdad needs a new hospital, and someone has to choose where it goes. There's a story people tell about how it was done.
The physician in charge had pieces of fresh meat hung up in different quarters of the city, then went around to look. Where the meat spoiled fastest, he reasoned, the air was worst.

Where it stayed fresh longest, the sick would heal best, and that's where the hospital should go. Whether it happened just that way, nobody can be sure; it comes from a later book of physicians' lives.
But it fits what else is told about him. His name was Abu Bakr al-Razi.

teach.b: Al-Razi means the man from Rayy, a city in Persia. He became a physician and led hospitals in Rayy and in Baghdad, and his habit was simple and stubborn: look first.
He kept notes on his patients, case after case: what they said, what he saw, what he gave them, what happened next.
After his death, his students gathered those notes into a huge book, al-Hawi, the comprehensive book, so later doctors could learn from his bedside.
One short work is on two diseases that came with fever and spots on the skin: smallpox and measles.

Al-Razi watched closely and wrote down how they differed: how each began, how the rash came out, which signs warned of danger. Told apart, they could be treated apart. That's the whole method in a sentence.
He also wrote that a doctor shouldn't trust only the books.
If what you see in a patient disagrees with what an old authority says, what's in front of you counts. And he didn't write only for doctors with hospitals behind them.
Al-Razi, the books say, wrote a little treatise for the poor: how to treat illness when there's no doctor and no money. Care for all who come, with your eyes open.

how: Muslim physicians such as al-Razi kept careful case notes and wrote treatises on telling diseases apart, and his writings were studied by later doctors.

games.q: you're choosing where to build a hospital in Baghdad. how do you decide?
o: pick the quarter closest to the palace.
hang meat across the city and see where it spoils slowest.
games.why: that's the story people tell about al-Razi: test the air, then build where it's best.

practice: Bring to mind a doctor or nurse who once looked at you closely, really looked, and saw what was wrong, or one who cared for someone you love.

Hold their face in mind and ask what they noticed that others missed, and how you might thank them, or someone like them. If you pray, you can pray for the people who heal; if not, just hold your gratitude.

wordCard.voice: Al-Razi. The physician who led hospitals in Rayy and Baghdad, kept notes at the bedside, and told smallpox from measles by looking closely. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: the one from Rayy, a city in Persia.

carryVoice: Your line: observe, then treat. Look first, and what's in front of you counts. That's day nine hundred twenty-one.
